question: A developer wants to keep the Bash tool available to Claude for most commands but ensure that destructive deletion commands are always blocked, even if the session later switches to bypassPermissions. Which configuration achieves exactly this?
options: A) disallowed_tools=["Bash"], which removes the Bash tool definition entirely so Claude can no longer see or attempt any Bash command
B) permission_mode="acceptEdits", which auto-approves filesystem commands like rm while still requiring a prompt for other Bash invocations
C) disallowed_tools=["Bash(rm *)"], which keeps Bash available but denies calls matching rm * in every permission mode, including bypassPermissions
D) allowed_tools=["Bash"] combined with permission_mode="default", which lets every Bash call reach the canUseTool callback for manual review
correct_answers: C) disallowed_tools=["Bash(rm *)"], which keeps Bash available but denies calls matching rm * in every permission mode, including bypassPermissions
explanations: Incorrect. A bare disallowed_tools=["Bash"] removes the entire tool, which prevents all Bash use, not just destructive deletion commands.
Incorrect. acceptEdits mode explicitly auto-approves filesystem commands including rm, which is the opposite of blocking destructive deletions.
Correct. A scoped deny rule like Bash(rm *) keeps the Bash tool usable while blocking only the matching destructive pattern, and deny rules apply even in bypassPermissions mode.
Incorrect. Routing every Bash call through canUseTool in default mode still allows a reviewer to approve an rm command, and it offers no protection once the mode is switched to bypassPermissions.
